summary: Specifies the Real-time Transport Object delivery over Unidirectional Transport protocol for robust delivery of application objects, such as files, DASH or HLS segments, or audio clips, to receivers over a one-way transport. It also supports low-latency streaming. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Like a radio broadcast of files and video, with no way for listeners to talk back.

questions: how does route deliver video over broadcast
what is forward error correction in route
subtitle: Reliable delivery of files and media over broadcast and multicast networks

tldr.problem: Broadcast and multicast networks send data in one direction only, but applications need reliable delivery of files and video segments. Receivers cannot request retransmission if packets are lost.
tldr.mechanism: ROUTE adds a delivery layer over UDP/IP that organizes Application Objects (files, video segments) into packets, includes Forward Error Correction (FEC) repair packets to recover from loss, and provides metadata signaling so receivers know how to reconstruct objects. It handles both real-time streaming (with latency constraints) and non-real-time downloads.
tldr.outcome: Informational: ROUTE is used by ATSC 3.0 television broadcast and DVB multicast services. The protocol is aligned with FLUTE (RFC 6726) but optimized for real-time media. It supports multiple delivery modes (files, entities, packages) and FEC schemes.

today: RFC 9223 is informational and has not been obsoleted. ROUTE is specified and deployed in the ATSC 3.0 broadcast television standard and in the DVB Adaptive Media Streaming over IP Multicast (DVB-MABR) specification. Services using ROUTE define profiles that constrain or extend the protocol features for their needs.

sections.title: Reliable Broadcasting of Objects
sections.content:
The Real-time Transport Object delivery over Unidirectional Transport (ROUTE) protocol enables robust delivery of Application Objects to receivers over broadcast or multicast networks. Application Objects are chunks of data meaningful to applications: files, MPEG DASH video segments, Apple HLS media segments, audio clips, or any other content.

Traditional networks like HTTP assume a two-way channel where a receiver can request retransmission of lost packets. Broadcast and multicast networks send data in one direction only; receivers cannot ask for retransmission. ROUTE solves this by adding Forward Error Correction: senders include extra repair packets that allow receivers to recover lost data without requesting it.

The protocol is designed for both real-time content (video and audio with timing constraints) and non-real-time content (files, applications). It can deliver sequences of related objects (like a series of video segments) in a timely manner, enabling services to consume the objects as they arrive.
sections.eli5: ROUTE is like a radio broadcast that automatically fixes errors. When the sender broadcasts a video segment and some packets get lost, the receiver can use extra correction packets to rebuild the missing pieces without asking the sender to repeat.

sections.title: How ROUTE Works
sections.content:
ROUTE builds on existing protocols: it uses the Layered Coding Transport (LCT) header format and packet structure from RFC 5651, runs over UDP/IP (supporting unicast, multicast, and broadcast), and leverages underlying security like IPsec if needed.

An Application Object is broken into a delivery-object or set of objects. These are packed into ROUTE packets, each with an LCT header that identifies the sender, the session, the object, and the position of the data in the object. A Codepoint field in the header indicates the type of payload: for example, initialization segments for video, media segments, or file data.

For recovery from packet loss, the sender creates repair packets using FEC (Forward Error Correction). If a receiver is missing packets, it can use repair packets to reconstruct the lost data. The sender also broadcasts session metadata (signaling information) so receivers know what is being sent, what objects are available, and how to interpret the packets.

Receivers collect packets in a cache and can then make the objects available to applications via HTTP, allowing traditional applications to work over broadcast/multicast without modification.
sections.eli5: The sender breaks up a file or video into chunks and puts each chunk in a packet with a label saying which object it belongs to and where in the object it goes. The sender also sends extra packets (repair packets) that contain the same information in a different way, so if you miss some packets, the repair packets let you rebuild them.

sections.title: ROUTE Packet Structure
sections.content:
A ROUTE packet carries a UDP header, an LCT header, a FEC Payload ID, and the payload data.

The LCT header includes:

  • Transport Session Identifier (TSI): identifies the session (e.g., one DASH Representation in a video stream).
  • Transport Object Identifier (TOI): identifies which object the packet belongs to (e.g., which video segment).
  • Codepoint: signals the type of content (file mode, entity mode, initialization segment, media segment, etc.).
  • Source Packet Indicator (SPI): 1 for source packets, 0 for repair packets.

The FEC Payload ID for source packets is a 32-bit start_offset field indicating the byte position of this packet's data within the object. For repair packets, it follows RFC 6330 FEC encoding information.

Optional header extensions can signal timing (when the sender sent this), object length (for early detection of completeness), and transmission timing information.

ROUTE supports codepoint values ranging from 0 to 255. Reserved values indicate file mode, entity mode, packages, and media segment types. Service-specific uses can define values 11–255.
sections.eli5: A ROUTE packet is like an envelope with labels: 'this is for session 5', 'it contains bytes 1000-2000 of object 3', 'it's a media segment', and 'here's some timing info'. If it's a repair packet instead, the envelope says 'I'm redundancy that helps you recover lost packets'.

sections.title: Delivery Object Modes
sections.content:
ROUTE defines four delivery modes, each suited to different application needs:

File Mode: Objects are described in an Extended File Delivery Table (EFDT), an enhanced version of the FDT from RFC 6726 (FLUTE). The EFDT can include a filename template that receivers use to reconstruct file names from object identifiers, maximum expiration times, and content types. Ideal for file delivery and non-real-time content.

Entity Mode: Metadata travels as HTTP-style entity headers alongside the object payload. The receiver extracts HTTP headers to learn about the object. Supports both simple objects and chunked content (like CMAF Chunks in video). Headers can indicate content length, media type, and other HTTP semantics.

Unsigned Package Mode: Multiple files are bundled into a single delivery object using MIME multipart format. The receiver unpacks the container and extracts individual files. Useful for delivering groups of related files at once.

Signed Package Mode: Similar to Unsigned Package, but the package includes signatures for validation using S/MIME (Secure MIME). Adds cryptographic proof of authenticity.
sections.eli5: ROUTE can deliver objects in different ways depending on what makes sense: file mode (send a table of contents), entity mode (send headers with the data), package mode (bundle files together), or signed package mode (bundle files and prove they're authentic).

sections.title: Forward Error Correction
sections.content:
ROUTE's robustness comes from Forward Error Correction (FEC). The sender produces source packets (the original data) and repair packets (redundancy information). If the receiver loses some source packets, it can use repair packets to recover the lost data.

FEC operates on Transport Objects (the delivery objects after packetization). For each delivery object, the sender creates a FEC transport object by concatenating the delivery object, padding octets, and a 4-byte size field. This is divided into FEC symbols of a fixed size.

A FEC super-object bundles multiple FEC transport objects together for combined protection. This allows one set of repair packets to protect multiple delivery objects, reducing overhead.

FEC Repair Flows are transport sessions carrying repair packets. A repair flow references one or more source flows and provides recovery symbols for them. Session metadata signals which FEC scheme to use (e.g., Reed-Solomon codes from RFC 6330), symbol sizes, and how objects are mapped to FEC symbols.

The document provides guidelines on FEC symbol size, super-object construction, and recovery timeout, but leaves specific scheme choices to service profiles (e.g., ATSC 3.0 or DVB profiles).
sections.eli5: With FEC, the sender sends some extra packets that are mathematical combinations of the original packets. If you lose a packet, you can use two extra packets to figure out what was in the lost one—like solving for an unknown in an equation.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
ROUTE itself does not define security mechanisms but can leverage underlying layer security: IPsec for confidentiality and integrity, or other transport-layer encryption. Services using ROUTE (like broadcast television) may add their own security mechanisms.

Since ROUTE broadcasts data to all receivers on a network (or multicast group), endpoints receive all packets whether intended for them or not. Applications must implement access control and encryption at a higher level if selective delivery is needed.

Metadata signaling can be delivered in-band (as ROUTE packets) or out-of-band (via other channels). Out-of-band signaling may allow operators to distribute metadata securely without exposing it in broadcast packets.

Privacy considerations include the fact that receivers cannot hide their membership in a multicast group or which objects they request, unlike unicast HTTP where requests are between two parties.
sections.eli5: ROUTE doesn't encrypt by itself—that's up to the broadcast service. Since broadcasts go to everyone, applications have to decide who gets to use the content, either by scrambling it or by distributing decryption keys only to authorized receivers.
